stem: On the eve of independence, the Indian economy under British rule was essentially:
options: A backward, stagnant, and largely agrarian (agricultural) economy, whose development had been retarded by colonial policies
The richest economy in the world
solution: On the eve of independence (1947), the Indian economy under nearly two centuries of British colonial rule was essentially a backward, stagnant, and largely agrarian (agricultural) economy — its development had been deliberately retarded by the colonial policies, which used India as a supplier of raw materials for British industry and a market for British manufactured goods. The economy suffered from low growth, low per capita income, widespread poverty, and technological backwardness. Understanding the backward, agrarian, colonial nature of the pre-independence economy is a key prelims point. On the eve of independence, India had a backward, stagnant, agrarian economy, retarded by British colonial policies.

stem: The basic aim of the British colonial government's economic policies in India was to:
options: Serve the interests of the British economy — using India as a source of raw materials and a market for British goods
solution: The basic aim of the British colonial government's economic policies in India was NOT the development of India, but the promotion of the interests of the British (home) economy. Under these policies, India was reduced to a supplier of cheap raw materials (like raw cotton, jute, indigo) for British industries, and a captive market for the finished manufactured goods produced in Britain. This colonial exploitation transformed and distorted India's economy to suit Britain's needs, and it stunted India's own economic development. Understanding the exploitative aim of British economic policy is a key prelims point. British colonial economic policy aimed to serve Britain's interests — making India a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods.

stem: The sector in which the largest proportion of India's population was engaged at the time of independence was:
solution: At the time of independence, agriculture was the sector in which the largest proportion of India's population was engaged — about 70–75% of the working population depended on agriculture for their livelihood. India was thus an overwhelmingly agrarian economy. Yet, despite so many people depending on it, agriculture was stagnant and backward (with low productivity), suffering from problems like the exploitative land-revenue systems, lack of irrigation and technology, and the pressure of population. Understanding that agriculture employed the bulk of the population is a key prelims point. At independence, agriculture engaged the largest share (about 70–75%) of India's population.

stem: The agricultural sector on the eve of independence was in a state of __________, with very low productivity.
solution: The agricultural sector on the eve of independence was in a state of stagnation (backwardness), with very low productivity (very low yield per hectare). This stagnation was caused by several factors: the exploitative land-revenue and land-tenure systems (especially the Zamindari system, which gave the landlords/intermediaries no incentive to improve the land while extracting high rents from the actual cultivators); the lack of irrigation, technology, fertilisers, and investment; the forced commercialisation of agriculture (growing cash crops for export rather than food); and the pressure of a growing population on the land. As a result, farm output barely grew, and Indian agriculture remained backward. Understanding the stagnation of colonial agriculture (and its causes) is a key prelims point. Agriculture at independence was stagnant, with very low productivity, due to the land-revenue systems and lack of investment/technology.

stem: The land settlement system introduced by the British in which zamindars (landlords) were made the owners of the land and had to collect and pay revenue was called the:
solution: The Zamindari system (also known as the Permanent Settlement, introduced by the British — Lord Cornwallis — in 1793, especially in Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha) was the land settlement in which the zamindars (landlords/intermediaries) were made the owners of the land, responsible for collecting the land revenue from the actual cultivators (tenants) and paying a fixed amount to the British government. The zamindars extracted high rents from the cultivators but had little interest in improving the land — which contributed greatly to the stagnation and misery of agriculture (the cultivators were left impoverished and with no incentive or means to improve). Understanding the Zamindari system (and its harmful effects on agriculture) is a key prelims point. The Zamindari (Permanent Settlement) system made zamindars the landowners/revenue-collectors, contributing to agricultural stagnation and the cultivators' misery.

stem: The British colonial policies led to the __________ (decline/ruin) of India's world-famous handicraft industries.
solution: The British colonial policies led to the de-industrialisation of India — the decline and ruin of India's world-famous traditional handicraft industries (like the fine cotton textiles/muslin of Bengal, and other handicrafts). This happened because: the British imposed heavy tariffs/duties on Indian goods entering Britain (and its markets) while allowing British machine-made goods to flood into India duty-free (or cheaply); and the cheap, machine-made British goods (from the Industrial Revolution) undercut and out-competed the Indian handmade products. As a result, India's handicrafts collapsed, throwing millions of artisans out of work (many of whom fell back on agriculture, increasing the pressure on the land) — and India was reduced from an exporter of manufactures to an exporter of raw materials. Understanding the de-industrialisation (ruin of handicrafts) is a key prelims point. British policies caused de-industrialisation — the decline and ruin of India's famous handicraft industries.

stem: The decline of the handicraft industries under British rule had the twofold effect of causing unemployment among artisans and:
options: making India dependent on imports of British manufactured goods (turning it into a market for Britain)
solution: The decline (de-industrialisation) of India's handicraft industries under British rule had a twofold (double) effect: (1) it caused massive unemployment among the traditional artisans and craftsmen (who lost their livelihoods, and many of whom were forced back onto agriculture, increasing the pressure on the land); and (2) it created a new demand in India for the manufactured (machine-made) goods that were now imported from Britain — turning India into a captive market (a dependent importer) for British manufactured products. So India, which had once been a great exporter of fine manufactures, was reduced to depending on British imports for manufactured goods. Understanding this twofold effect of de-industrialisation is a prelims point. The decline of handicrafts both threw artisans out of work AND made India a dependent market for British manufactured imports.

stem: The industrial sector in India on the eve of independence was:
options: Underdeveloped/limited (with only a few industries, like cotton and jute textiles), lacking capital and basic/heavy industries
solution: The industrial sector in India on the eve of independence was underdeveloped and limited. Although some modern industries did develop (starting from the second half of the 19th century) — notably the cotton textile industry (mainly in the west, Maharashtra/Gujarat, with Indian capital) and the jute textile industry (in Bengal, mostly under foreign/British ownership), and later the iron and steel industry (Tata Iron and Steel Company, TISCO, established in 1907) — the industrial base remained very narrow: there was a serious lack of capital-goods (heavy/basic) industries (industries that make machines and materials to produce other goods), a low contribution of industry to national income, and little public-sector investment. So industrialisation was slow, limited, and lopsided. Understanding the limited, underdeveloped state of colonial industry is a key prelims point. India's industrial sector at independence was underdeveloped and limited (only a few industries, and lacking basic/heavy industries and capital).

stem: The first iron and steel company established in India (in 1907), an important step in Indian industry, was:
solution: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was established in 1907 (at Jamshedpur), and it was a landmark in the development of Indian industry — one of the few basic/heavy industries set up during the colonial period, and with Indian capital and enterprise (founded by the Tata family). Its establishment showed that Indians could set up modern heavy industry. However, such industries were few, and overall the industrial base remained narrow under colonial rule. Understanding that TISCO (1907) was the first iron and steel company is a prelims point. The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO), established in 1907, was the first iron and steel company in India.

stem: India's foreign trade under British rule was characterised by the export of __________ and the import of finished manufactured goods.
options: primary products / raw materials (like raw cotton, jute, indigo, tea)
solution: India's foreign trade under British rule was characterised by the export of primary products and raw materials — such as raw cotton, jute, indigo, tea, sugar, and food grains — and the import of finished/manufactured goods (like cotton textiles, machinery, and other manufactures) from Britain. So India was reduced to an exporter of cheap raw materials and an importer of expensive finished goods — a classic colonial trade pattern that suited Britain's economy (feeding its industries and selling to India's market) but harmed India's own development. Understanding this colonial trade pattern (raw materials out, manufactures in) is a key prelims point. Under British rule, India exported primary products/raw materials and imported finished manufactured goods.

stem: A large part of India's foreign trade was controlled by Britain, and India's export surplus was used to make 'unrequited' payments to Britain (a drain of wealth), including for:
options: the expenses of the British administration, war costs, and 'Home Charges' (with no corresponding benefit to India)
solution: A large part of India's foreign trade was controlled by Britain, and India generally had an export surplus (it exported more than it imported). But this surplus did NOT bring gold or benefits into India; instead, it was used to make 'unrequited' payments to Britain — that is, payments for which India got nothing in return. These included the expenses of the British administration in India, the costs of British wars, pensions and salaries of British officials, and the 'Home Charges' (payments India had to make to Britain). This one-way outflow of India's wealth to Britain, with no corresponding benefit, is what the Indian nationalists (like Dadabhai Naoroji) called the 'Drain of Wealth' — a major cause of India's impoverishment. Understanding the 'Drain of Wealth' (export surplus used for unrequited payments to Britain) is a key prelims point. India's export surplus was drained away to Britain as 'unrequited' payments (administration, wars, Home Charges) — the 'Drain of Wealth'.

stem: The nationalist leader who put forward the 'Drain of Wealth' theory (that Britain was draining/exploiting India's wealth) was:
solution: Dadabhai Naoroji (known as the 'Grand Old Man of India') was the nationalist leader and economist who developed and popularised the 'Drain of Wealth' theory — the argument (in his famous work 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India') that Britain was continuously draining away/exploiting India's wealth (through the unrequited transfers to Britain), which was impoverishing India and was the root cause of its poverty. This theory was a powerful critique of colonial rule. Understanding that Dadabhai Naoroji gave the Drain of Wealth theory is a prelims point. Dadabhai Naoroji put forward the 'Drain of Wealth' theory, arguing that Britain was draining India's wealth.

stem: The demographic (population) condition of India before independence was characterised by:
options: High birth rates AND high death rates, high infant mortality, low life expectancy, and widespread illiteracy
solution: The demographic (population) condition of India before independence was characteristic of a backward, poor economy (the 'first stage' of demographic transition): both the birth rate and the death rate were very high (around 48 and 40 per thousand, respectively); infant mortality (deaths of infants) was very high (about 218 per thousand); life expectancy was very low (only about 32 years); and literacy was very low (only about 16%, with female literacy far lower). These conditions reflected the widespread poverty, disease (frequent epidemics and famines), malnutrition, and lack of health care and education under colonial rule. Understanding these demographic features (high birth/death rates, low life expectancy, low literacy) is a key prelims point. Pre-independence India had high birth and death rates, high infant mortality, very low life expectancy (~32 years), and low literacy (~16%).

stem: The overall rate of growth of India's economy (and per capita income) during the colonial period was:
solution: The overall rate of growth of India's economy (aggregate output) during the colonial period was very low — near stagnation — and the growth of per capita income (income per person) was even lower (barely any growth, or close to zero, over the last half-century of colonial rule). Studies (like those of the economist V.K.R.V. Rao) estimated that aggregate output grew at less than 2% a year, and per capita output at only about half a per cent a year, during the first half of the 20th century. This near-stagnant growth, combined with a rising population, kept the vast majority of Indians in poverty. Understanding the very low (near-stagnant) growth of the colonial economy is a key prelims point. India's economic growth (and per capita income growth) during the colonial period was very low — near stagnation.

stem: The occupational structure (distribution of the workforce among sectors) during the colonial period showed:
options: Little change — agriculture remained the largest employer (about 70–75%), with a small and stagnant industrial/manufacturing share
solution: The occupational structure (the distribution of the working population among the different sectors — agriculture, industry, and services) showed little change during the colonial period, and it remained highly lopsided: agriculture remained by far the largest employer, engaging about 70–75% of the workforce throughout, while the share of the manufacturing (industrial) sector was small and stagnant (around 10%), and the services sector accounted for the rest (around 15–20%). Moreover, there were regional variations. The persistence of such a large share in (backward) agriculture and the failure of industry to absorb more workers reflected the economy's stagnation. Understanding the unchanging, agriculture-dominated occupational structure is a prelims point. The colonial occupational structure changed little — agriculture stayed the largest employer (~70–75%), with a small, stagnant industrial share.

stem: One of the FEW positive contributions of British rule (though built to serve British interests) was the development of the:
options: Railways (and some other infrastructure like roads, ports, telegraph)
solution: One of the few positive contributions of British rule was the development of some infrastructure — most notably the railways (introduced in 1853), and also roads, ports, water transport, and the posts and telegraph. However, this infrastructure was developed primarily to serve British interests — to help transport raw materials from the interior to the ports (for export to Britain) and to distribute British manufactured goods, and for administrative and military control — rather than for the benefit of the Indian people. Still, the railways did have some unintended benefits for India (breaking geographical barriers, promoting some trade and mobility). Understanding that the railways/infrastructure were a positive (but self-serving) British contribution is a prelims point. The development of the railways (and some other infrastructure) was a positive contribution of British rule, though built mainly to serve British interests.

stem: The railways were introduced in India in 1853. Their MAIN purpose, from the British point of view, was to:
options: Facilitate the transport of raw materials to the ports (for export) and the movement of British goods and troops
solution: The railways were introduced in India in 1853 (the first railway line ran from Bombay to Thane). From the British point of view, their main purpose was to serve British colonial and commercial interests: to facilitate the transport of India's raw materials from the interior to the ports (so they could be exported to Britain) and to distribute British manufactured goods to the Indian markets in the interior, as well as to move British troops and administer the country (for control). So, although the railways were an important development, they were built primarily to strengthen British exploitation and control — not for India's own development (though they did have some incidental benefits for India). Understanding the colonial purpose of the railways is a prelims point. The railways (1853) were built mainly to move raw materials to the ports, distribute British goods, and move troops — serving British interests.

stem: At the time of independence, India was a net importer of __________, reflecting the failure of colonial agriculture to feed the population.
solution: At the time of independence, India was a net importer of food grains — that is, it could not grow enough food to feed its own population and had to import food grains. This reflected the failure and stagnation of agriculture under colonial rule: despite most of the population being engaged in farming, agricultural productivity was so low (and much good land had been diverted to cash crops for export, and the population had grown) that India faced food shortages and had to import food. (This food-scarcity problem was a major challenge that independent India had to overcome — later addressed by the Green Revolution.) Understanding that colonial India was a net food-grain importer is a prelims point. At independence, India was a net importer of food grains, reflecting the failure of colonial agriculture to feed the population.

stem: The commercialisation of agriculture under British rule (growing cash crops like indigo, cotton, and jute for the market/export) generally:
options: Was often forced and served British industry — and it did not benefit the farmers, who often grew cash crops instead of food (worsening food shortages)
solution: The commercialisation of agriculture under British rule — the shift toward growing cash crops (like indigo, raw cotton, jute, tea, and opium) for the market and for export — was often forced upon the farmers and served the interests of British industry and trade (supplying raw materials to British factories), rather than benefiting the Indian farmers. The farmers usually did not gain from it (they were paid low prices, and in cases like indigo were coerced and exploited); and importantly, growing these non-food cash crops (instead of food crops), together with the export of food, meant less food was available for the people — contributing to food shortages and famines. So commercialisation, as it occurred under colonialism, was largely exploitative and harmful. Understanding the exploitative nature of colonial agricultural commercialisation is a prelims point. Colonial commercialisation of agriculture (cash crops for export) was often forced, served British industry, and did not benefit farmers — and it worsened food shortages.

stem: Assertion (A): India's handicraft industries declined under British rule. Reason (R): Britain imposed heavy duties on Indian goods while flooding India with cheap machine-made British goods. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India's handicraft industries declined (de-industrialisation) under British rule. And the reason is (R) that Britain, to protect its own industries and sell its goods, imposed heavy tariffs/duties on Indian handmade goods (making them uncompetitive in British and other markets) while flooding the Indian market with cheap, machine-made British goods (from its Industrial Revolution) that undercut and displaced the Indian handicrafts. This discriminatory trade policy is exactly what ruined the Indian handicrafts — so R correctly explains A. Understanding this cause of de-industrialisation is a prelims point. India's handicrafts declined because Britain taxed Indian goods heavily while flooding India with cheap British machine-made goods.

stem: During the colonial period, the FIRST attempt to estimate India's national income was made by:
solution: During the colonial period, the first attempt to estimate India's national income was made by Dadabhai Naoroji. (Other individuals — like William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao, and R.C. Desai — also made such estimates.) Among all these colonial-era estimates, the work of V.K.R.V. Rao was considered the most significant and acceptable. But the pioneering first attempt was by Dadabhai Naoroji. These estimates all pointed to India's very low per-capita income and slow growth. Understanding that Dadabhai Naoroji made the first national-income estimate (and V.K.R.V. Rao's was the most acceptable) is a prelims point. Dadabhai Naoroji made the first attempt to estimate India's national income in the colonial period; V.K.R.V. Rao's estimate was the most acceptable.

stem: The colonial-era national-income estimate considered the MOST significant/acceptable was made by:
solution: Among the various national-income estimates made during the colonial period (by Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao, and R.C. Desai), the estimate by V.K.R.V. Rao was considered the most significant and acceptable (the most scientific and reliable) for its time. Rao's careful estimates helped confirm the very low level and near-stagnant growth of India's national and per-capita income under colonial rule. Understanding that V.K.R.V. Rao's national-income estimate was the most acceptable is a prelims point. V.K.R.V. Rao's colonial-era estimate of India's national income was the most significant/acceptable.

stem: The three main land-revenue (land settlement) systems introduced by the British in India were the Zamindari, the Mahalwari, and the __________ system.
solution: The three main land-revenue systems introduced by the British in India were: (1) the Zamindari system (Permanent Settlement) — where the zamindars (landlords) owned the land and collected revenue (in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, etc.); (2) the Mahalwari system — where the revenue was settled with the village or estate ('mahal') as a whole (in parts of the Ganga valley, north-west, etc.); and (3) the Ryotwari system — where the settlement was made directly with the individual cultivator ('ryot'), who was recognised as the owner and paid revenue directly to the state (in the Madras and Bombay Presidencies, introduced by Thomas Munro). All three systems generally extracted high revenue and left the actual cultivators impoverished, contributing to agricultural stagnation. Understanding the three land-revenue systems (Zamindari, Mahalwari, Ryotwari) is a prelims point. The three main British land-revenue systems were the Zamindari, the Mahalwari, and the Ryotwari system.

stem: In the Ryotwari system of land revenue, the settlement (and payment of revenue) was made directly with the:
solution: In the Ryotwari system, the land-revenue settlement was made directly with the individual cultivator (the 'ryot'), who was recognised as the owner of the land and paid the revenue directly to the government (state), without any intermediary landlord (zamindar). This system was introduced mainly in the Madras and Bombay Presidencies (associated with Thomas Munro and Alexander Read). Although it removed the middleman, the revenue demanded was still high (and could be revised), so the cultivators remained burdened and often fell into debt. Understanding the Ryotwari system (direct settlement with the cultivator) is a prelims point. In the Ryotwari system, the land-revenue settlement was made directly with the individual cultivator (ryot).

stem: In the Mahalwari system, the land revenue was settled/assessed on the basis of the:
options: village or estate ('mahal') as a whole
solution: In the Mahalwari system, the land revenue was settled and assessed on the basis of the village or estate — the 'mahal' — as a whole (the village community was collectively responsible for paying the revenue, usually through the village headman). This system was introduced in parts of North India — the Ganga valley, the North-Western Provinces, parts of Central India and Punjab. Like the other systems, it too generally imposed a heavy revenue burden. Understanding the Mahalwari system (revenue settled with the village/mahal) is a prelims point. In the Mahalwari system, land revenue was assessed on the village or estate ('mahal') as a whole.

stem: During the colonial period, the jute textile industry (mostly located in Bengal) was largely under the ownership/control of:
solution: During the colonial period, the jute textile industry — concentrated mainly in Bengal (in and around Calcutta) — was largely under the ownership and control of foreigners (mostly British). This is in contrast to the cotton textile industry (concentrated in the western regions of Maharashtra and Gujarat), which was largely owned and run by Indians. So the two major textile industries had contrasting ownership — cotton mostly Indian, jute mostly foreign. Understanding that the jute industry was mostly foreign-owned is a prelims point. During the colonial period, the jute textile industry (in Bengal) was largely foreign (British)-owned.

stem: The cotton textile industry during the colonial period was concentrated mainly in the western regions of India (Maharashtra and Gujarat) and was largely owned by:
solution: The cotton textile industry during the colonial period was concentrated mainly in the western regions of India — in the states/regions of Maharashtra and Gujarat (cities like Bombay/Mumbai and Ahmedabad) — and it was largely owned and run by Indians (Indian entrepreneurs and capital). This contrasts with the jute industry (in Bengal), which was mostly foreign-owned. The cotton textile industry (along with jute, and later iron and steel) was one of the few modern industries that developed in colonial India. Understanding that the cotton textile industry was concentrated in the west and Indian-owned is a prelims point. The colonial cotton textile industry was concentrated in western India (Maharashtra, Gujarat) and was largely Indian-owned.

stem: A serious weakness of India's industrial development under colonial rule was the almost complete absence of __________ industries (industries that produce machines and materials to make other goods).
solution: A serious weakness (drawback) of India's industrial development under colonial rule was the almost complete absence of capital goods industries — the basic/heavy industries that produce machine tools, machinery, and materials used to produce other goods (i.e., the industries needed to build up and support further industrialisation). Apart from a few consumer-goods industries (like cotton and jute textiles) and the limited iron and steel (TISCO), India had hardly any industries making the machines and equipment for industry. Without such capital-goods industries, the industrial base remained narrow and dependent, and India could not become self-reliant in industry. Understanding the absence of capital-goods industries is a key prelims point. A key weakness of colonial industry was the near-absence of capital goods (basic/heavy) industries.

stem: The first railway line in India (1853) ran between:
solution: The first railway line in India was opened in 1853 and ran between Bombay (Mumbai) and Thane (a distance of about 34 km). This marked the beginning of the railways in India — an important development of the colonial period (though built mainly to serve British commercial, administrative, and military interests). The railway network then expanded across the country in the following decades. Understanding that the first railway (1853) ran from Bombay to Thane is a prelims point. The first railway line in India (1853) ran between Bombay (Mumbai) and Thane.

stem: The railways had a positive UNINTENDED effect on India by:
options: breaking down geographical barriers, fostering the mobility of people and the growth of trade/commerce across the country
solution: Although the railways were built to serve British interests, they had some positive unintended effects on India: they broke down the geographical barriers (connecting distant parts of the vast country), fostered the mobility of people (allowing people to travel long distances, undertake pilgrimages, and migrate for work), and promoted the growth of trade and commerce across the country (moving goods over long distances, creating a wider national market). (However, this same commercialisation also had a negative side — it helped drain raw materials out and bring British goods in.) So the railways had a mixed impact — with these positive unintended benefits alongside the harmful colonial purposes. Understanding the positive unintended effects of the railways is a prelims point. The railways positively (if unintentionally) broke geographical barriers and fostered the mobility of people and the growth of trade.

stem: The share of the agricultural sector in India's national income at the time of independence was:
solution: At the time of independence, the agricultural sector accounted for the largest share of India's national income — a little over 50% (roughly 50–55%). This reflected the agrarian nature of the economy (agriculture being the mainstay, though a backward one). The remaining national income came from the small industrial/manufacturing sector and the services sector. (Over the decades after independence, as the economy developed, the share of agriculture in national income declined, while that of industry and — especially — services rose.) Understanding that agriculture had the largest share (~50%+) of national income at independence is a prelims point. At independence, agriculture accounted for the largest share (a little over 50%) of India's national income.

stem: The world-famous fine cotton textile (muslin) that was ruined by British policy was especially associated with which city?
solution: The world-famous fine cotton textile — the exquisite muslin — that was ruined by British colonial policy was especially associated with Dhaka (Dacca) in Bengal (now the capital of Bangladesh). Dhaka muslin (and Bengal's fine cotton textiles generally) had been renowned throughout the world for its extraordinarily fine quality. The British policies (heavy duties on Indian textiles, and the flooding of India with cheap machine-made British cloth) destroyed this famous handicraft industry, throwing its skilled weavers into ruin — a striking example of de-industrialisation. Understanding that Dhaka was famous for muslin (ruined under the British) is a prelims point. The world-famous fine muslin cotton textile, ruined under British policy, was especially associated with Dhaka (Dacca) in Bengal.

stem: The British East India Company gained a foothold and began establishing control in India after the Battle of Plassey (1757). British rule then lasted until:
solution: The British East India Company gained a decisive foothold and began establishing its control over India after the Battle of Plassey (1757). British rule over India (first under the East India Company, and, after 1858, directly under the British Crown) then continued until 15 August 1947, when India became independent. So British domination of India lasted nearly two centuries (from the mid-18th century to 1947) — a long period during which the colonial economic policies shaped (and distorted) India's economy. Understanding the span of British rule (roughly 1757 to 1947) is a prelims point. British rule in India lasted from around the Battle of Plassey (1757) until independence in 1947 — nearly two centuries.

stem: The literacy rate in India at the time of independence was extremely low, at about:
solution: The literacy rate in India at the time of independence was extremely low — only about 16% (i.e., only about one in six people could read and write). Female literacy was far lower still (only about 7%). This very low literacy reflected the colonial neglect of mass education among the Indian people, and it was one of the serious social handicaps (along with poor health) that independent India inherited. Understanding that literacy was only ~16% at independence is a prelims point. The literacy rate at independence was only about 16% (with female literacy about 7%).

stem: The life expectancy (average expected lifespan) of an Indian at the time of independence was only about:
solution: The life expectancy (the average number of years a person could expect to live) at the time of independence was only about 32 years — extremely low (compared with today's figure of around 70 years). This very low life expectancy reflected the poverty, malnutrition, disease (frequent epidemics), high infant mortality, and near-total lack of health care and public-health facilities under colonial rule. It was one of the poor social/demographic conditions that independent India had to improve. Understanding that life expectancy was only ~32 years at independence is a prelims point. Life expectancy at independence was only about 32 years.

stem: The infant mortality rate (deaths of infants per 1000 born) in India at independence was:
solution: The infant mortality rate (the number of infant deaths per 1000 live births) in India at the time of independence was very high — about 218 per thousand (i.e., more than one in five babies died in infancy). This alarmingly high infant mortality (compared with a much lower figure today) reflected the widespread poverty, malnutrition, disease, and near-total absence of medical care and public-health facilities for the masses under colonial rule. It was part of the grim demographic picture inherited by independent India. Understanding the very high infant mortality (~218 per 1000) at independence is a prelims point. Infant mortality at independence was very high — about 218 per thousand.

stem: Which of the following was a positive (if incidental) legacy of British rule for India?
options: The introduction of the railways, a unified administrative structure, and English education (which, though serving colonial aims, had some lasting benefits)
solution: While British rule was, on the whole, exploitative and harmful to India's economy, it did leave a few positive (if incidental, and largely self-serving) legacies, such as: the introduction of the railways (and some roads, ports, posts, and the telegraph); a unified administrative and legal structure across the country (which had some role in fostering national unity); and the introduction of English education (and the English language), which — though meant to serve colonial administration — gave some Indians access to modern knowledge and ideas (and later became a link language and an asset in the modern world). These were incidental benefits, arising as by-products of colonial rule rather than from any intention to develop India. Understanding these incidental positive legacies is a prelims point. Positive (incidental) legacies of British rule include the railways, a unified administrative structure, and English education.

stem: The great famine that struck Bengal in 1943 (during colonial rule), killing about three million people, highlighted the:
options: terrible failure and neglect of the colonial economy (food shortages, poverty, and administrative failure)
solution: The great Bengal Famine of 1943, in which about three million people died of starvation, was one of the worst human tragedies of colonial rule, and it starkly highlighted the terrible failure and neglect of the colonial economy: the food shortages and mass poverty produced by decades of exploitative policies, together with wartime disruptions and the colonial government's administrative failure and indifference (including the diversion of food and failure to provide relief). The famine underscored the deep failures of the colonial economy in even ensuring food security for the people. Understanding the significance of the 1943 Bengal Famine is a prelims-relevant point. The Bengal Famine of 1943 (about 3 million deaths) highlighted the failure and neglect of the colonial economy.

stem: The land-revenue systems (like the Zamindari) contributed to the misery of the cultivators mainly because:
options: the revenue/rent demanded was very high and rigid (had to be paid regardless of the harvest), impoverishing the cultivators and giving intermediaries no incentive to improve the land
they gave land free to farmers
solution: The land-revenue systems (like the Zamindari/Permanent Settlement) contributed greatly to the misery of the cultivators and the stagnation of agriculture mainly because: the revenue (or rent) demanded was very high and rigid — it had to be paid by fixed dates regardless of whether the harvest was good or bad (so even in years of drought/crop failure, the full amount was extracted, ruining the cultivators); this impoverished the actual tillers of the soil, leaving them no surplus to invest in the land; and, in the Zamindari system, the intermediary zamindars (who profited from the rents) had no incentive to invest in or improve the land (they gained regardless). So these systems drained the cultivators, discouraged improvement, and kept agriculture backward. Understanding how the revenue systems caused agricultural misery/stagnation is a prelims point. The land-revenue systems impoverished cultivators because the revenue was high and rigid, and intermediaries had no incentive to improve the land.

stem: Overall, the occupational structure and the economy at independence show that India was in the __________ stage of economic development.
solution: Overall, the occupational structure (with about 70–75% of the workforce in agriculture and only a small share in industry) and the other features of the economy at independence (low per-capita income, stagnation, low literacy and life expectancy, high birth and death rates, food shortages) show that India was in an early/underdeveloped stage of economic development — a backward, agrarian economy. India displayed the classic characteristics of an underdeveloped/developing economy: heavy dependence on a backward agriculture, an underdeveloped industrial sector, low income and living standards, and poor human-development indicators. Overcoming this backwardness was the great challenge before independent India. Understanding that India was at an early/underdeveloped stage at independence is a prelims point. At independence, India was a backward, agrarian economy in an early/underdeveloped stage of economic development.

stem: Which economic historian wrote 'The Economic History of India' and, like Dadabhai Naoroji, exposed the exploitative nature of British colonial economic policy?
solution: R.C. Dutt (Romesh Chunder Dutt) was the Indian economic historian and nationalist who wrote 'The Economic History of India', in which he documented and exposed the exploitative nature of British colonial economic policy and its damaging effects on the Indian economy (the ruin of handicrafts, the burden of the land revenue, the drain of wealth, and the resulting poverty). Along with Dadabhai Naoroji (with his 'Drain of Wealth' theory), R.C. Dutt was a pioneer of the nationalist economic critique of British rule. Understanding that R.C. Dutt wrote the Economic History of India (critiquing colonial policy) is a prelims-relevant point. R.C. Dutt wrote 'The Economic History of India', exposing the exploitative nature of British colonial economic policy.

stem: The suffering of the peasants forced to grow indigo (for British planters) — later the scene of Mahatma Gandhi's first satyagraha in India — was in:
solution: The suffering of the peasants forced (by British planters) to grow indigo (a cash crop, used for blue dye) under an exploitative system was especially severe in Champaran (in Bihar). The peasants were compelled to grow indigo on part of their land and sell it at very low prices, keeping them in poverty. This exploitation led to Mahatma Gandhi's first satyagraha (civil-resistance movement) in India — the Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 — in which he successfully took up the cause of the indigo cultivators. This is a famous example of the exploitative forced commercialisation of colonial agriculture (and of the freedom struggle). Understanding the Champaran indigo episode is a prelims-relevant point. The exploitation of peasants forced to grow indigo was severe in Champaran (Bihar), the scene of Gandhi's first satyagraha (1917).

stem: During the colonial period, modern industry began to develop in India in the:
solution: During the colonial period, modern (machine-based) industry began to develop in India in the second half of the 19th century (from about the 1850s–1860s onward). This began with the cotton textile mills (in the west) and the jute mills (in Bengal), followed later by the iron and steel industry (TISCO, 1907) and, in the 20th century, a few other industries (sugar, cement, paper). However, this industrial growth was slow and limited, and the industrial base remained narrow (lacking capital-goods industries). Understanding that modern industry began in the second half of the 19th century is a prelims point. Modern industry in India began to develop in the second half of the 19th century (cotton and jute mills, later iron and steel).

stem: In the second phase of colonial industrial growth (the interwar period), a few more industries came up, such as:
solution: In the later phase of colonial industrial growth (roughly the interwar period — the 1920s and 1930s), a few more industries came up in India, notably the sugar, cement, and paper industries (and some others), adding a little to the earlier base of cotton textiles, jute, and iron and steel. However, the overall industrial development remained slow and limited (and still lacked the vital capital-goods industries), so India's industrial base stayed narrow at independence. Understanding that sugar, cement, and paper industries developed in this period is a prelims point. In the later colonial period, industries like sugar, cement, and paper came up (adding to the earlier textiles and iron & steel).

stem: The excessive dependence of the population on agriculture (with industry unable to absorb workers) meant that Indian agriculture suffered from __________ (too many people working the land, more than needed).
options: disguised unemployment / overcrowding on the land
solution: The excessive dependence of the population on agriculture — because the ruined handicrafts and the underdeveloped industry could not absorb the workers — meant that far more people were engaged in (crowded onto) agriculture than were actually needed to work the land. This resulted in disguised unemployment (also called 'hidden' unemployment): many people appeared to be employed in farming, but their contribution to output was little or nothing (they could be removed without reducing production), because the land was overcrowded with surplus labour. This overcrowding on the land lowered productivity per worker and kept the rural population in poverty. Understanding disguised unemployment/overcrowding in colonial agriculture is a prelims point. Excessive dependence on agriculture caused disguised unemployment — too many people crowded onto the land, more than needed.

stem: The colonial government's investment in India's social sectors (health and education) was:
options: very limited/negligible (leading to poor health and education among the people)
solution: The colonial government's investment in India's social sectors — health and education (and other welfare) — was very limited and negligible. The British spent very little on public health, sanitation, and medical facilities, and very little on educating the Indian masses. As a result, the Indian people suffered from poor health (rampant disease, high mortality, low life expectancy) and very low literacy (only ~16%). This neglect of the social sectors was part of the broader colonial pattern of not investing in India's genuine development and welfare — and it left independent India with the heavy task of building up health and education from a very low base. Understanding the colonial neglect of health and education is a prelims point. The colonial government's investment in health and education was very limited, leaving the people with poor health and low literacy.

stem: At the time of independence, the __________ sector (of the three broad sectors) contributed the least to national income and employment.
solution: At the time of independence, the manufacturing/industrial (secondary) sector contributed the least to national income and employment among the three broad sectors — because industry was so underdeveloped and limited under colonial rule. Agriculture (the primary sector) dominated both national income (a little over 50%) and employment (~70–75%); the services (tertiary) sector had a modest share; and the industrial/manufacturing sector was the smallest and weakest (contributing only a small share of income and employing only about a tenth of the workforce). This reflected the failure of industrialisation under colonialism. Understanding that industry was the smallest sector at independence is a prelims point. At independence, the manufacturing/industrial sector contributed the least to national income and employment.

stem: The chief BENEFICIARY of India's colonial economy (its raw materials, markets, and drained wealth) was:
solution: The chief beneficiary of India's colonial economy was Britain (the British economy, industry, and ruling class). The whole colonial system was designed so that India served Britain's interests: India supplied cheap raw materials for British industries; India was a captive market for British manufactured goods; India's wealth was drained to Britain (through the unrequited payments — the 'Drain of Wealth'); and even the infrastructure (like railways) was built to facilitate this exploitation. The Indian people — the farmers, artisans, and workers — were the losers, kept in poverty. So Britain gained at India's expense. Understanding that Britain was the chief beneficiary of the colonial economy is a prelims point. The chief beneficiary of India's colonial economy was Britain (its economy and industry), at India's expense.

stem: The enormous challenges that the colonial economy left for independent India included overcoming poverty, food shortages, low literacy, poor health, and:
options: backward agriculture and a weak industrial base (i.e., the need to modernise agriculture and industrialise the economy)
solution: The colonial economy left independent India with enormous challenges to overcome, including: widespread poverty and low per-capita income; food shortages (India was a food importer); very low literacy (~16%) and poor education; poor health and low life expectancy (~32 years); and — fundamentally — a backward, stagnant agriculture (needing modernisation and land reforms to raise productivity) and a weak, narrow industrial base (needing rapid industrialisation, especially the building of basic/heavy industries, to develop the economy and become self-reliant). Tackling these inherited problems — modernising agriculture, industrialising, and improving the people's welfare — became the central tasks of independent India's economic planning and development. Understanding the challenges inherited from the colonial economy is a key prelims-relevant point. Independent India inherited the challenges of overcoming poverty, food shortages, low literacy, poor health, backward agriculture, and a weak industrial base.

stem: Assertion (A): India's per-capita income grew very slowly during the colonial period. Reason (R): The economy's total output grew very slowly (near stagnation) while the population kept growing. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India's per-capita income (income per person) grew very slowly (almost not at all) during the colonial period. And the reason is (R) that the economy's total (aggregate) output grew very slowly — near stagnation (less than 2% a year) — while at the same time the population kept growing. Since per-capita income is total output divided by population, a near-stagnant total output shared among a growing population means the income per person barely grew (it grew at only about half a per cent a year). So the slow output growth combined with population growth is exactly why per-capita income stagnated — R correctly explains A. Understanding this reasoning is a prelims point. Per-capita income grew very slowly under colonialism because output grew near stagnation while the population kept rising.

stem: The system of agriculture on the eve of independence suffered from low productivity mainly because of the lack of irrigation, technology, and:
options: proper investment and incentive to invest (due to the land-revenue system and intermediaries)
solution: Colonial agriculture stagnated because of low levels of technology, lack of irrigation and, crucially, the absence of investment and incentives caused by the exploitative land-revenue systems that transferred surplus to intermediaries.

stem: Under the Zamindari system (Permanent Settlement of 1793), the amount of revenue the zamindar had to pay was:
options: fixed permanently, regardless of the actual harvest
solution: The Permanent Settlement fixed the revenue permanently; whatever the harvest, the zamindar had to pay the fixed amount, forcing him to squeeze the peasants even in bad years.

stem: The Ryotwari system of land revenue was introduced mainly in which regions of British India?
options: Madras and Bombay Presidencies (the south and west)
solution: The Ryotwari system, in which revenue was settled directly with the individual cultivator (ryot), was prevalent mainly in the Madras and Bombay Presidencies.

stem: Dadabhai Naoroji presented his 'Drain of Wealth' theory in his famous book titled:
options: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
solution: Dadabhai Naoroji expounded the drain of wealth theory in his work 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'.

stem: The reason India became an exporter of raw materials and an importer of finished goods under British rule was that Britain wanted India to serve as:
options: a supplier of cheap raw materials and a market for British manufactured goods
solution: Colonial trade policy deliberately made India a source of cheap raw materials (like cotton, jute, indigo) and a captive market for finished British manufactures, ruining Indian industry.

stem: The person whose estimate of India's national income during the colonial period is regarded as the most significant/reliable was:
solution: Among the several colonial-era estimates, the one prepared by V.K.R.V. Rao (during 1931-32) is regarded as the most significant and methodologically sound.

stem: During the colonial period, India's average annual growth of aggregate real output was estimated at less than:
solution: The aggregate real output grew at less than 2% a year during the first half of the 20th century, with per capita growth barely above 0.5% — near stagnation.

stem: The suffix industries were almost absent under colonial rule; India particularly lacked __________ goods industries needed to produce machines.
solution: India lacked capital-goods industries (industries that produce machine tools and equipment to make other goods), which severely limited industrial self-reliance.

stem: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was established in 1907 at:
solution: TISCO was set up in 1907 at Sakchi (later Jamshedpur) in present-day Jharkhand, becoming a landmark in India's industrial history.

stem: The occupational structure of colonial India remained largely unchanged, with about __________ of the population dependent on agriculture.
solution: Around 70-75% of the working population depended on agriculture throughout the colonial period, showing the economy's lack of structural change.

stem: A striking regional feature of the colonial occupational structure was that agricultural dependence DECREASED in some regions such as:
solution: In parts of the Madras, Bombay and Bengal Presidencies the dependence on agriculture declined (with a rise in manufacturing/services), while in Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab it actually increased.

stem: The systematic de-industrialisation of India under British rule refers to the:
options: decline and ruin of India's traditional handicraft industries without a corresponding growth of modern industry
solution: De-industrialisation was the deliberate decline of India's world-famous handicrafts (especially textiles) coupled with the failure to develop a modern industrial base to replace them.

stem: The fine Indian textiles (like muslin) lost their world market under British rule partly because of:
options: heavy tariffs on Indian goods in Britain and the flooding of India with cheap machine-made British cloth
solution: Discriminatory British tariff policy taxed Indian textiles heavily in Britain while allowing cheap Manchester machine-made cloth to flood India, destroying Indian handicrafts.

stem: The 'drain of wealth' during colonial rule refers to the fact that a part of India's national wealth/income was:
options: siphoned off to Britain without any adequate economic/material return to India
solution: The drain of wealth was the export of a large part of India's product and revenue to Britain (for administrative costs, war expenses, and profits) without an equivalent return, impoverishing India.

stem: India's demographic transition is said to have entered its second decisive decade after which census year, treated as a 'year of great divide'?
solution: The year 1921 is called the 'Year of the Great Divide' for India's population, after which the population began to grow steadily (mortality fell), marking the second stage of demographic transition.

stem: The overall literacy rate in India at the time of independence was about:
solution: The overall literacy rate was a mere 16% at independence, and female literacy was around 7%, reflecting colonial neglect of education.

stem: Life expectancy at birth in India at the time of independence was only about:
solution: Life expectancy was extremely low, around 32 years, at independence, indicating very poor health conditions.

stem: The infant mortality rate at the time of independence was as high as about:
solution: The infant mortality rate was about 218 per thousand live births at independence — a marker of the very poor health infrastructure.

stem: The famine that struck Bengal in 1943, killing about three million people, exposed the failure of the colonial administration in the area of:
solution: The Bengal Famine of 1943 revealed the colonial government's failure to ensure food security and manage the distribution of food grains, causing mass starvation deaths.

stem: The jute textile industry under colonial rule was concentrated in Bengal and was largely dominated by:
solution: The jute industry, centred in Bengal, was mostly owned and controlled by foreigners (the British), unlike the cotton textile industry which had more Indian ownership.

stem: The cotton textile industry during the colonial period was concentrated mainly in which regions?
solution: The cotton textile mills were concentrated in the western parts of India — Maharashtra (Bombay) and Gujarat (Ahmedabad) — and were largely owned by Indians.

stem: The first railway line in India, opened in 1853, ran between Bombay and:
solution: India's first railway line (1853) ran from Bombay to Thane, a distance of about 34 km.

stem: The railways, though built to serve British interests, had a positive unintended effect on India by:
options: breaking down geographical/cultural barriers and fostering national unity and commercialisation
solution: The railways, while designed to move raw materials and troops for the British, unintentionally promoted the mobility of people, national integration and the commercialisation of agriculture.

stem: The commercialisation of agriculture under British rule (growing cash crops for export) often harmed the peasants because:
options: they were forced to grow cash crops (like indigo) instead of food, worsening food insecurity, and got little of the profit
solution: Forced cash-cropping (e.g., indigo) diverted land from food crops and left peasants poorer and food-insecure, while the profits went to British planters and traders.

stem: Mahatma Gandhi's first satyagraha in India (1917), concerning the plight of indigo cultivators, took place in:
solution: The Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 in Bihar was Gandhiji's first satyagraha in India, against the oppressive indigo (tinkathia) system imposed on peasants.

stem: The economic historian who, like Naoroji, exposed British exploitation in his work 'The Economic History of India' was:
solution: Romesh Chandra (R.C.) Dutt wrote 'The Economic History of India', documenting the drain and the destructive effects of colonial economic policy.

stem: The 'de-industrialisation' had a two-fold effect: it ruined the handicraft industries AND:
options: forced artisans back onto already overcrowded agriculture, increasing pressure on land
solution: As handicrafts collapsed, unemployed artisans were pushed back to agriculture, increasing the burden on land and worsening disguised unemployment.

stem: Which of the following was NOT a positive contribution (even if incidental) of British rule?
options: An efficient administrative and legal system
Introduction of the telegraph and post
solution: India did NOT achieve rapid or self-reliant industrialisation under the British; railways, administration, and the telegraph/post were among the incidental positive legacies.

stem: 'Disguised unemployment' in colonial (and post-colonial) Indian agriculture means:
options: more people working on the land than actually needed, so that some contribute little or nothing to output
solution: Disguised unemployment exists when more workers are engaged in agriculture than required, so that removing some would not reduce output — their marginal productivity is near zero.

stem: During the colonial period, the FIRST person to attempt an estimate of India's national income was:
solution: Dadabhai Naoroji made the first attempt to estimate India's national income; later Findlay Shirras, William Digby and V.K.R.V. Rao also made estimates.

stem: Under the Mahalwari system, the land revenue was assessed and collected on the basis of the:
options: estate/village (mahal) as a unit, with the village headman collecting it
solution: In the Mahalwari system, revenue was assessed on the mahal (a village or a group of villages) as a whole, and the village community/headman was responsible for its collection.

stem: The share of India's manufacturing/modern industry in the national income at independence was:
options: very small (only a few per cent)
solution: The modern industrial sector's contribution to national income was very small at independence, reflecting the limited and lopsided industrial development under colonial rule.

stem: The famous fine muslin cloth ruined by British policy was especially associated with which city in Bengal?
solution: Dhaka (in Bengal, now in Bangladesh) was world-famous for its fine muslin, whose industry was destroyed by British colonial policy.

stem: India's foreign trade under British rule generated a large export surplus, but this surplus did NOT benefit India because it was:
options: used to make 'unrequited' payments to Britain (for administration, wars, and the drain)
saved as gold reserves in India
solution: Despite a large export surplus, India got no corresponding gold/silver inflow; the surplus was used to finance the colonial administration, wars, and the drain of wealth to Britain.

stem: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, affected India's colonial trade by:
options: reducing the distance and cost of trade between India and Britain, intensifying British commercial control
solution: The opening of the Suez Canal shortened the sea route between India and Britain, reducing transport costs and tightening British commercial exploitation of India.

stem: Which crop was India a major EXPORTER of during the colonial period?
options: Raw cotton, jute, indigo, tea and food grains
solution: India exported primary products — raw cotton, jute, indigo, tea, sugar and food grains — while importing finished manufactured goods from Britain.

stem: The main reason the British developed the railways, ports and telegraph in India was to:
options: facilitate the exploitation of India — moving raw materials to ports and British goods inland, and controlling the territory
solution: Infrastructure like railways, ports and the telegraph was built primarily to serve British commercial and administrative/military interests, not Indian development.

stem: At independence, India was a net IMPORTER of food grains, which showed that:
options: colonial agriculture had failed to feed the growing population
there was no agriculture in India
solution: India had to import food grains at independence, reflecting the stagnation and low productivity of colonial agriculture, which could not feed the population.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes the industrial structure at independence?
options: Limited to a few consumer-goods industries (like cotton, jute), with almost no capital-goods or heavy industry
solution: Industry was confined mainly to a few consumer-goods industries such as cotton and jute textiles, with virtually no capital-goods or basic/heavy industries.

stem: The colonial government's investment in the social sectors of health and education was:
options: dismally low, resulting in poor literacy and health
solution: Public expenditure on health and education under colonial rule was extremely low, leaving India with mass illiteracy and very poor health at independence.

stem: British rule in India, from the Battle of Plassey (1757) and Company control, formally ended in:
solution: British colonial rule ended with India's independence on 15 August 1947.

stem: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched (land-revenue system and its key feature)?
options: Zamindari — revenue settled with the individual cultivator
Ryotwari — revenue settled directly with the cultivator (ryot)
solution: In the Ryotwari system, revenue was settled directly with the individual cultivator (ryot). The Zamindari/Permanent Settlement made zamindars owners with fixed revenue; Mahalwari settled with the village.

stem: The 'commercialisation of agriculture' did have one effect that could be seen as modernising, namely:
options: the beginnings of a shift from subsistence farming toward production for the market
solution: Commercialisation began a shift from subsistence to market-oriented (cash-crop) farming; but under coercion it mostly harmed peasants and worsened food security.

stem: The stagnation of per capita income during the colonial era was because:
options: aggregate output grew very slowly while population grew, so income per head barely rose
solution: Both aggregate output and per capita income grew very slowly (near stagnation) as the small growth in output was offset by population growth.

stem: The chief beneficiary of the colonial Indian economy — its raw materials, captive market, and drained wealth — was:
solution: Colonial economic policy was designed to benefit Britain, which extracted India's raw materials, used India as a market, and drained its wealth.

stem: Which of the following was a key CHALLENGE that the colonial legacy left for independent India?
options: Widespread poverty, food shortages, illiteracy, poor health, and a stagnant agrarian economy
solution: Independent India inherited mass poverty, food insecurity, low literacy, poor health and a backward, stagnant, agriculture-dependent economy — the challenges its planners had to tackle.

stem: Which of the following BEST states the central conclusion of the chapter on the eve of independence?
options: Colonial rule modernised and enriched India
Two centuries of colonial rule left India a backward, stagnant, semi-feudal agrarian economy, with de-industrialised handicrafts, drained wealth, and mass poverty
India was already an industrial power in 1947
British rule had no economic effect on India
solution: The chapter concludes that British colonial rule left India economically backward and stagnant — with ruined handicrafts, low agricultural productivity, drained wealth, and widespread poverty and illiteracy.

stem: The transformation of the economy that British policy prevented was the shift of the workforce from agriculture into:
solution: Colonial policy blocked the normal structural shift of workers from agriculture into modern industry and services, keeping India's occupational structure frozen and agriculture-heavy.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence' is that:
options: The British developed India into a rich, modern economy

Nearly two centuries of British colonial rule left India, at independence, a backward, stagnant, and impoverished economy — with a stagnant agrarian sector, a ruined handicraft/de-industrialised base, an underdeveloped industrial sector, a drained and exploited trade, and poor demographic and social conditions — leaving independent India with enormous challenges to overcome
India was better off under British rule
The colonial economy had no problems
solution: The chapter conveys that nearly two centuries of British colonial rule, whose policies were designed to serve Britain's interests rather than India's development, left India — on the eve of independence in 1947 — a backward, stagnant, and impoverished economy. Its key features were: an agricultural sector that was the mainstay of the people (employing ~70–75%) yet was stagnant and had very low productivity (due to the exploitative land-revenue systems like the Zamindari system, lack of investment and technology, and forced commercialisation); a ruined handicraft base (de-industrialisation), which threw artisans out of work and made India a dependent market for British manufactures; an underdeveloped and limited industrial sector (only a few industries, and lacking basic/heavy industries and capital); a foreign trade that was controlled by Britain and drained India's wealth (the export of raw materials and the import of finished goods, with an export surplus used for 'unrequited' payments to Britain — the 'Drain of Wealth' described by Dadabhai Naoroji); very low overall and per-capita growth (near stagnation); and poor demographic and social conditions (high birth and death rates, high infant mortality, low life expectancy of ~32 years, and low literacy of ~16%). Although British rule did leave some infrastructure (like the railways, built mainly to serve British interests), the net effect was to distort and hold back India's economy. Understanding this backward, exploited colonial economy — and the enormous challenges it left for independent India — is the central concern of this chapter. Two centuries of British colonial rule left India, at independence, a backward, stagnant, drained, and impoverished economy, posing huge challenges for the new nation.
